newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: MOTORCYCLING-DOOHAN STILL HUNGRY FOR SUCCESS.
newsitem.headline: MOTORCYCLING-DOOHAN STILL HUNGRY FOR SUCCESS.

text.p: Nine years ago during his first season on the motorcycling Grand Prix circuit, Michael Doohan said he would quit at the age of 32.
Just days before his self-imposed deadline expiring this Wednesday, the three times world 500cc champion was having second thoughts.
"I still love racing," the Australian Honda rider said in an interview. "I haven't really decided if I'll be around next year, but I don't feel I'm ready to leave it all behind yet."
Despite his greying hair and a battered right leg, which almost needed amputation after a high-speed crash at Assen in 1992, Doohan is still hungry for success.
"My goal is to beat everyone. Nothing beats the instant satisfaction of winning a race," he said.
"If I'm not winning, or at least in the top 10, then I'm unhappy and I can't sleep."
This year, Doohan will enjoy untroubled slumber.
He has won four of the five races so far and finished second in the other, taking a commanding 31-point lead over Spanish team mate Alex Criville.
Doohan said the accident, which has forced him to use a bike with a special hand break, has also changed his approach to life.
"The accident did change a lot. I am still able to race with the same intensity, however, now I try to live my private life with more intensity.
"It changed the way I approach things in life. I try not to get wound up about things anymore," said Doohan, a known introvert who spends his spare time on his boat in Monaco.
It also stopped him worrying about records, although he is now second in the all-time list of 500cc winners behind Italian Giacomo Agostini with his victory at Sunday's Austrian Grand Prix.
"To have achieved 38 wins is fantastic, but records are not important. What is important is to enjoy every minute of every race and live for the moment.
"The day will come when someone will overtake me in the list, or even overtake Agostini's 68 wins," he said. "My hair is quite grey already so I don't think I'll be around that long."
Doohan could also become the third rider only after Agostini and Britain's Mike Hailwood to lift four successive world titles.
"My dream was to win back-to-back titles. After doing so in 1994 and 1995 I was satisfied," he said.
"Winning the title is a great reward at the end of the season but not as thrilling as winning a race."
When Doohan does end his illustrious career he would like to help youngsters in their mental preparation.
"When I started I got no help. I had to learn everything by myself. I think I can help young aspiring riders in their mental approach towards the sport.
"I know I have helped Criville a lot. Everything he does is what I would do," Doohan said about his younger team mate and greatest rival for this year's title.
At the moment, the Queenslander appears to be far from retirement. But when the day does come, he hopes he will love the sport as much as he did when he entered his first race at the age of nine.
"I want to quit feeling good and not because I'm not good anymore. I want to quit while I'm still on the top," he said, adding "I will only ever race for Mick Doohan and no one else."
